blocks.text:
Design an online coding judge, the system behind a platform like LeetCode, that accepts a user's arbitrary, untrusted source code for a given problem, runs it safely against a set of test cases, and returns a verdict, accepted, wrong answer, or one of several failure modes. Every prior design in this project coordinated trusted, internal services. This one is fundamentally different: its core input is arbitrary code written by an unknown, unvetted stranger, and that code must be executed at all, safely, without ever being allowed to affect the host machine, another user's submission, or the platform itself.

The technique that makes this safe is strict sandbox isolation, no network access, a restricted filesystem, and hard, enforced CPU-time and memory ceilings, so that whatever the submitted code actually tries to do, the damage it can cause is always contained to its own single, disposable sandbox.

Every prior design in this project coordinated trusted, internal services. This one is fundamentally different: its core input is arbitrary code written by an unknown, unvetted stranger, and that code must be executed at all, safely, without ever being allowed to affect the host machine, another user's submission, or the platform itself.

The technique that makes this safe is strict sandbox isolation, no network access, a restricted filesystem, and hard, enforced CPU-time and memory ceilings, so that whatever the submitted code actually tries to do, the damage it can cause is always contained to its own single, disposable sandbox.

blocks.text: A user should be able to submit source code in one of several supported languages for a specific problem. The system should compile the code if needed and run it against every one of that problem's test cases. A clear verdict should be returned, accepted if every test case passes, or the specific failure reason, wrong answer, time limit exceeded, memory limit exceeded, runtime error, or compile error, and at which test case it first occurred. During a live contest, verdicts should feed a leaderboard ranking participants by problems solved and time taken.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first is what makes this design fundamentally unlike every other one in this project.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and the first is what makes this design fundamentally unlike every other one in this project.

blocks.alt: Strong sandbox isolation, deterministic and fair judging, massively parallel judging, low judging latency, and resistance to malicious code

blocks.text: Strong sandbox isolation means untrusted, arbitrary code must never be able to affect the host machine or any other user's submission, no matter what it tries to do. Deterministic and fair judging means the exact same submission must always receive the exact same verdict, since a nondeterministic judge would be a fundamentally broken one. Massively parallel judging means millions of independent submissions can be judged with zero coordination needed between them, the opposite constraint from the stock exchange design's per-symbol serialization. Low judging latency means a submitter expects a verdict back within a few seconds under normal load. And resistance to malicious code means code that deliberately tries to exhaust resources, reach the network, or escape its sandbox must be safely contained every single time.

Low judging latency means a submitter expects a verdict back within a few seconds under normal load. And resistance to malicious code means code that deliberately tries to exhaust resources, reach the network, or escape its sandbox must be safely contained every single time.

blocks.text: This design assumes judging stops at the first failing test case, matching how most real coding judges operate, rather than scoring partial credit across every test case. Each problem defines its own time and memory limits, enforced identically regardless of submission language. Sandbox isolation is assumed to be provided by a container or equivalent OS-level isolation mechanism, with no network access and a restricted, read-only filesystem beyond the submission's own working directory, covered further in section 21.

blocks.text: A large coding platform might judge hundreds of thousands of submissions per day in steady state, spiking to tens of thousands per minute during a popular live contest. Because every submission judges entirely independently, with no shared state between them, this workload is embarrassingly parallel, unlike almost every other design in this project. A typical verdict is expected back within a few seconds of submission, dominated by actual execution time against test cases rather than queueing delay, as long as the sandbox worker pool keeps pace with submission volume.

blocks.text: A submission enters through the submission API and is placed on a queue, from which a scheduler assigns it to an available sandbox drawn from a warm pool. The sandbox compiles the code if needed and runs it against every test case in isolation, reporting each test case's output, execution time, and memory usage to the judge, which determines the final verdict and, for a live contest, updates the leaderboard.

Code that exceeds a limit or attempts something forbidden is simply killed, with the damage contained entirely to that one disposable sandbox.

blocks.alt: Untrusted code runs inside an isolated sandbox with no network access and hard resource ceilings; anything that exceeds a limit or attempts a forbidden action is killed, contained entirely within that one sandbox

blocks.text: For each test case, the judge checks, in order, whether the submission failed to compile or crashed, whether it exceeded its time limit, whether it exceeded its memory limit, and only then whether its actual output matches the expected output. The first check that fails determines that test case's outcome, and judging stops there rather than continuing to later test cases.

blocks.alt: Each test case is checked in order for a crash or compile failure, then a time limit violation, then a memory limit violation, and only then an output mismatch, with the first failure determining the verdict

blocks.text: Starting a fresh, fully isolated sandbox from scratch for every single submission would be slow enough that startup cost alone could dominate total judging time. Instead, a pool of already-initialized sandboxes sits ready, and a submission is assigned whichever one is currently free, reset to a clean state after each use.

blocks.alt: A cold sandbox started from scratch for every submission is slow, dominated by startup cost; a pool of pre-warmed, reset-after-use sandboxes lets a submission start judging almost immediately

A sandbox worker crashing mid-judge is detected by a missing acknowledgment, and the same submission is safely re-assigned to a healthy worker rather than being lost

blocks.text: The happy path is the submit flow above, an available sandbox runs the submission cleanly against every test case, and the judge returns accepted. The workflow worth walking through separately is a sandbox worker crashing partway through judging, perhaps due to a submission that genuinely destabilizes its own sandbox. Because the queue only removes a submission once its assigned worker acknowledges completion, a crash before that acknowledgment simply leaves the submission eligible for redelivery, and a different, healthy sandbox worker picks it up and judges it correctly, with the user seeing only a slightly delayed verdict rather than a lost submission.

TIME_LIMIT_MILLIS = 1000
MEMORY_LIMIT_MB = 256


class TestCase:
    # One test case: the input description (for display) and its expected output.
    def __init__(self, input_description, expected_output):
        self.input_description = input_description
        self.expected_output = expected_output


class ExecutionResult:
    # What a sandbox reported for one test case's execution: the actual output
    # produced, time and memory used, and whether it crashed outright.
    def __init__(self, actual_output, time_used_millis, memory_used_mb, crashed):
        self.actual_output = actual_output
        self.time_used_millis = time_used_millis
        self.memory_used_mb = memory_used_mb
        self.crashed = crashed


class Judge:
    # Applies verdict logic to a sandbox's reported results: checks each test
    # case in order for a crash, then a time limit violation, then a memory
    # limit violation, and only then an output mismatch, stopping at the first failure.
    def __init__(self, time_limit_millis, memory_limit_mb):
        self.time_limit_millis = time_limit_millis
        self.memory_limit_mb = memory_limit_mb

    def evaluate(self, test_cases, results):
        for i, (test_case, result) in enumerate(zip(test_cases, results)):
            case_number = i + 1  # 1-indexed, for a human-readable verdict message

            if result.crashed:
                return f"RUNTIME_ERROR at test case {case_number}"
            if result.time_used_millis > self.time_limit_millis:
                return f"TIME_LIMIT_EXCEEDED at test case {case_number}"
            if result.memory_used_mb > self.memory_limit_mb:
                return f"MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED at test case {case_number}"
            if result.actual_output != test_case.expected_output:
                return f"WRONG_ANSWER at test case {case_number}"

        return "ACCEPTED"  # every test case passed every check


def main():
    test_cases = [
        TestCase("[2,7,11,15], target=9", "[0,1]"),
        TestCase("[3,2,4], target=6", "[1,2]"),
        TestCase("[3,3], target=6", "[0,1]"),
    ]

    judge = Judge(TIME_LIMIT_MILLIS, MEMORY_LIMIT_MB)

    # Submission A: correct output on every test case, well within resource limits.
    results_a = [
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 200, 20, False),
        ExecutionResult("[1,2]", 210, 20, False),
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 190, 20, False),
    ]
    print("Submission A:", judge.evaluate(test_cases, results_a))

    # Submission B: wrong output on the second test case; judging should stop there.
    results_b = [
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 200, 20, False),
        ExecutionResult("[1,3]", 210, 20, False),
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 190, 20, False),
    ]
    print("Submission B:", judge.evaluate(test_cases, results_b))

    # Submission C: exceeds the time limit on the very first test case.
    results_c = [
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 1500, 20, False),
        ExecutionResult("[1,2]", 210, 20, False),
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 190, 20, False),
    ]
    print("Submission C:", judge.evaluate(test_cases, results_c))

    # Submission D: exceeds the memory limit on the first test case.
    results_d = [
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 200, 300, False),
        ExecutionResult("[1,2]", 210, 20, False),
        ExecutionResult("[0,1]", 190, 20, False),
    ]
    print("Submission D:", judge.evaluate(test_cases, results_d))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: ["Architecture: submissions queued to a warm pool of isolated sandboxes, judged against test cases with strict resource limits, feeding a submission store and, for live contests, a leaderboard.","Capacity: hundreds of thousands of submissions judged per day, spiking to tens of thousands per minute during a live contest, judged in a fully embarrassingly parallel way.","The core techniques: strict sandbox isolation for untrusted code, and ordered verdict logic (crash, then time limit, then memory limit, then output match), both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.","Database: a problem and test case store read far more than written, alongside an append-heavy, user-partitioned submission store.","End-to-end workflows: a normal submit-and-judge flow and a worker-crash re-queue flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.","Consistency: a deterministic, exact verdict for every submission, paired with an eventually consistent live-contest leaderboard.","Trade-offs: a fresh container per submission versus a warm sandbox pool versus no real sandboxing at all, compared directly on isolation strength and startup latency."]
items: Architecture: submissions queued to a warm pool of isolated sandboxes, judged against test cases with strict resource limits, feeding a submission store and, for live contests, a leaderboard.
Capacity: hundreds of thousands of submissions judged per day, spiking to tens of thousands per minute during a live contest, judged in a fully embarrassingly parallel way.

The core techniques: strict sandbox isolation for untrusted code, and ordered verdict logic (crash, then time limit, then memory limit, then output match), both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a problem and test case store read far more than written, alongside an append-heavy, user-partitioned submission store.
End-to-end workflows: a normal submit-and-judge flow and a worker-crash re-queue flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a deterministic, exact verdict for every submission, paired with an eventually consistent live-contest leaderboard.
Trade-offs: a fresh container per submission versus a warm sandbox pool versus no real sandboxing at all, compared directly on isolation strength and startup latency.
